Title: Ainet0: AI Forecasting Based Carbon Neutral Cloud Resource Management for Net Zero Targets

ABSTRACT
Cloud computing is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to optimize resource management and address
the complex and fluctuating demands of modern cloud environments. In particular, accurate CPU usage prediction-achieved
through appropriate time-series forecasting, is crucial for minimizing both over-provisioning and under-provisioning of cloud
resources. High predictive accuracy not only mitigates operational inefficiencies but also aligns with net-zero emission goals by
reducing unnecessary energy consumption. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework AINet0, which uses AI
forecasting models such as neural networks and time-series models for a dynamic resource management approach. The AINet0
integrates and examines Amazon’s DeepAR+ and Convolutional Neural Network-Quantile Regression (CNN-QR) within the
Amazon Web Services environment, aiming to enhance energy efficiency and sustainability to enable carbon-neutral cloud ser-
vices. We evaluated the AINet0 framework using a real testbed, CloudAIBus, and compared its performance against established
baselines. The experimental results demonstrate that the AINet0 enhances forecasting accuracy, achieving lower metrics such as
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), allowing for more precise resource allocation. Furthermore, performance evaluation
conducted on the Grid Workload Archive-T-12 dataset shows that the proposed models outperform traditional methods, enabling
more sustainable and cost-effective operations that further support net-zero emissions objectives.

Introduction
Recent advancements in large-scale Artificial Intelligence (AI)
have facilitated the remarkable progress of highly successful
applications such as large language models (LLMs) like Ope-
nAI’s GPT and High-Flyer’s DeepSeek, and protein structure pre-
diction models like DeepMind’s AlphaFold [1–3]. These inno-
vations have fundamentally transformed how people work and
study [4–7]. At the same time, their widespread adoption has
heightened the demand for computing resources, much of which
is fulfilled by cloud services that can provide substantial com-
putational capacity [8]. The carbon footprint of cloud services
cannot be overlooked due to their substantial energy demands

1.1

Motivation
The rapid expansion of AI applications has not only advanced
capabilities in areas such as natural language processing and
healthcare innovation [18–20], but has also led to a dramatic
increase in computational demands [21]. As the computational
demands of these AI applications, particularly distributed train-
ing and inference workloads, rely heavily on cloud infrastructure,
contributing significantly to energy consumption and carbon
emissions [22, 23]. For instance, data centres account for 2% of
global electricity use, with AI workloads exacerbating this foot-
print through energy-intensive computing operations [10, 24].
This environmental impact conflicts with sustainability goals,
such as the UK’s commitment to achieving net-zero carbon
emissions by 2050 [25, 26].
While cloud computing enables scalable and ample comput-
ing resources, traditional resource allocation methods often
fail to balance efficiency with dynamic demand, leading to
over-provisioning (energy waste) or under-provisioning (ser-
vice level agreement violations) [27, 28]. Recent efforts to
address these challenges, such as Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM)-based predictive scaling [29, 30], improved energy effi-
ciency but lacked investigation in quantifying economic and envi-
ronmental trade-off [31]. Advanced forecasting models such as
DeepAR+ and CNN-QR offer greater potential, with DeepAR+
excelling at modeling seasonal and long-term temporal depen-
dencies, while CNN-QR provides robust quantile estimates for
uncertainty-aware provisioning [32]. When deployed via man-
aged services like Amazon Forecast, these models can automate
resource allocation with higher accuracy, reducing prediction
errors and operational costs [33]. For example, enterprises such
as Anaplan and Foxconn achieved substantial cost savings using
Amazon Forecast for demand-aware resource planning, high-
lighting Amazon Forecast’s capacity and viability for sustainable
cloud operations [34, 35].
The dual pressures of both escalating AI-driven computing
resource demands and urgent sustainability net-zero targets
underscore the need for resource allocation frameworks that
optimize operational and environmental outcomes. While exist-
ing methods demonstrate partial success in cost or energy
efficiency, their study in adapting dynamic workloads remains
a critical gap in achieving scalable and low-carbon cloud oper-
ations [36]. This research aims to address this challenge by
integrating resource forecasting with cloud infrastructure,
promoting precise resource provisioning that aligns real-time
demand with sustainability targets.
1.2
|
Contributions
We propose the AINet0 framework to incorporate DeepAR+
and CNN-QR within AWS infrastructure, enabling probabilistic
forecasting for dynamic CPU resource utilization. This approach
addresses both short-term demand fluctuations and long-term
uncertainty, directly linking prediction accuracy to energy effi-
ciency. The goal of this research is to provide valuable insights
for cloud service providers by developing a model with reduced
prediction error. The key contributions of this paper are:
• Advanced Uncertainty-Aware Forecasting Methodol-
ogy: Proposed AI-based resource management framework
AINet0 using forecasting models such as DeepAR+ and
CNN-QR, to reduce provisioning errors for sustainable cloud
computing.
• Analysis of Stationarity Challenge: Through stationarity
testing, we identify and mitigate non-stationary patterns in
cloud workloads, a critical challenge to reliable forecasting.
• Real Testbed and Implementation Environment: We
implemented and tested AINet0 using the real testbed
CloudAIBus [33] within Amazon Forecast environment.
• Comparative Performance Analysis: Performed compar-
ative analysis of error metrics among proposed algorithms as
well as with baselines to examine model performance.
1.3
|
Paper Organization
The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews
related work on AI-driven resource management strategies.
Section 3 presents the methodology, architecture design, and
explanation about DeepAR+, CNN-QR, and stationarity analysis.
Section 4 describes the experimental setup, presents performance
evaluation and compares experimental results with baselines,
and discusses the outcomes. Section 5 concludes the paper, high-
lighting potential future work on enhancing forecasting models
and expanding their applications to other domains within cloud
computing.

Related Works
Research on CPU resource prediction has evolved significantly,
with an increasing emphasis on improving accuracy and address-
ing the dynamic nature of cloud workloads. Early research
focused on resource provisioning to balance cost and QoS in
fluctuating demand scenarios. Calheiros et al. [37] proposed
an AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA)-based
workload prediction for Software as a Service (SaaS) providers,
aiming to dynamically allocate cloud resources in response to
variable user demand. Their framework achieved up to 91% pre-
dictive accuracy in simulations, improving resource utilization
efficiency with minimal QoS degradation. However, this work did
not explicitly analyze stationarity assumptions or their impact on
model performance, leaving challenges about robustness under
highly volatile workloads.
Janardhanan et al. [38] introduce an algorithm for predicting
CPU load using Google Cluster trace data, comparing the per-
formance of ARIMA and LSTM models. Their work highlights
the performance of LSTM in handling CPU usage prediction,
particularly for unstable and non-linear data. They demonstrate

LSTM’s potential to improve scheduling efficiency and energy
utilization in large-scale cloud environments. Wang et al. [17]
proposed the AmazonAICloud framework, which leverages
Amazon Chronos-a pre-trained time-series model, for proactive
CPU utilization forecasting in cloud environments deployed
via AWS SageMaker. The work highlights the limitations of
traditional models such as ARIMA and LSTM by evaluating
Amazon Chronos against ARIMA, LSTM, and DeepAR, which
underscores the potential of pre-trained, scalable AI models to
streamline deployment in a cloud environment while promoting
cloud sustainability goals.
Tang et al. [39] introduced Fisher, a framework combining a
metrics selection module with a Bidirectional LSTM (BI-LSTM)
to predict container CPU load in cloud environments. By clus-
tering metrics based on shape similarity, Fisher reduced input
dimensionality while maintaining accuracy, achieving a sub-
stantially lower MAPE compared to ARIMA and conventional
LSTM models. Rao et al. [40] compared ARIMA, Holt-Winters,
and LSTM on a custom 410-point CPU utilization dataset.
Their experiment demonstrates that LSTM achieved the lowest
MAPE, outperforming ARIMA due to its capacity to model
non-linear fluctuations, highlighting LSTM’s capacity for unsta-
ble CPU data despite inherent seasonality. Nashold et al. [41]
analyzed Seasonal AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Aver-
age (SARIMA) and LSTM for CPU forecasting using a dataset
from Microsoft Azure. Their results suggest that SARIMA
excelled in long-term predictions by leveraging seasonal pat-
terns, while LSTM outperformed in short-term forecasts. This
research emphasized SARIMA’s dependency on stationarity
assumptions, whereas LSTM demonstrated robustness against
non-stationary workloads. Velu et al. [33] proposed a DeepAR
model-based framework for proactive resource allocation in
cloud environments. The framework addresses both station-
ary and non-stationary time-series data, ensuring efficient and
accurate CPU usage predictions. Their framework implemented
on Google Colab demonstrated superior performance over
LSTM and ARIMA baselines, achieving significant reductions in
MAE, MAPE, and MSE, which managed to reduce unused CPU
resources from 98.65% to 32.35%, highlighting its effectiveness
in minimizing over-provisioning. However, this research did
not build the link between prediction accuracy and operational
outcomes, which are required to understand its impact on global
net-zero objectives.
2.1
|
Critical Analysis
Table 1 highlights the primary differences between our proposed
AINet0 system and existing AI forecast frameworks. Existing
CPU resource forecasting approaches exhibit limitations in
addressing the challenges of non-stationary workloads and
scalable, sustainable resource allocation. While early models
like ARIMA [37] and LSTM [38] improved prediction accu-
racy by assuming stationarity, limiting their adaptability to
dynamic cloud environments. Hybrid frameworks like Fisher
[39] advanced the field with Bi-LSTM, but they remain con-
strained by limited scalability in real environments. Our work
addresses these gaps through AINet0, which examines both
DeepAR+ and CNN-QR and handles both stationary and
non-stationary workloads through Augmented Dickey-Fuller
(ADF) and Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS) tests,
ensuring effectiveness against volatile demand patterns. Further-
more, our work provides insight into the link between prediction
accuracy and operational outcomes, aiming to promote global
net-zero objectives.

3.1
|
Deepar+
The DeepAR+ model is a probabilistic forecasting algorithm
based on autoregressive recurrent neural networks (RNNs),
specifically designed for large-scale time-series datasets [32]. The
DeepAR+ model is developed by Amazon using a large amount
of time-series data and is trained using random sampling and
can effectively recognise trends and seasonality. Unlike tradi-
tional methods such as ARIMA, which require per-series param-
eter tuning, DeepAR+ trains a single unified model across all
VM traces in the dataset, leveraging shared temporal patterns to
improve generalization. This enables the DeepAR+ model learns
from previous datasets and can adapt to new data with a shorter
historical record, giving it a significant advantage over classical
methods.
3.2
|
CNN-QR
The CNN-QR model is developed by Amazon based on the
CNN to predict scalar time-series data [32]. It employs a quan-
tile decoder to generate probabilistic forecasts, constructing a
global model capable of handling complex datasets. Similar to
DeepAR+, CNN-QR captures information from related time
series, identifying seasonality and other key behavioral com-
ponents. The model’s design involves evaluating the quality of
reconstructed outputs from the quantile decoder relative to the
encoded inputs, which uses quantile regression to extract features
from the CNN, thereby enhancing its predictive capability.

Initial data preprocessing involves parsing timestamps (convert-

Feature engineering was applied to extract additional tempo-

speed may indirectly contribute to resource over-provisioning by
delaying resource adjustments.
3.3.1
|
Time Series Analysis
By considering trend, seasonality, and noise components, time
series decomposition provides valuable information on the
underlying structure of the dataset. In this study, we employ Sea-
sonal and Trend decomposition based on LOESS (STL), which
begins with a smoothing step to break down the data. As illus-
trated in Figure 5, the seasonal component’s magnitude varies lin-
early with time rather than exponentially. This approach reveals
that the dataset contains daily repeating seasonal cycles and sig-
nificant noise, highlighting the importance of further stationarity
testing to understand the dataset’s dynamics.

Performance Evaluation
In this section, we discuss model training, evaluation metrics,
experimental setup, baselines, and results.
4.1
|
Model Training
In the model training phase, we focused on employing the
DeepAR+ and CNN-QR algorithms provided by Amazon
Forecast. Each predictor was trained independently, with the
necessary hyperparameters configured for a one-hour horizon
to predict CPU usage for each VM. Backtesting against historical
data was applied to evaluate model performance, identify dis-
crepancies, and refine the models to enhance predictive accuracy.
Additionally, feature engineering was implemented to address
missing data, ensuring that the models remained effective even

The selection of MAPE, RMSE, and WAPE is intended to pro-
vide a comprehensive evaluation of prediction accuracy. Metrics
like MAPE and WAPE that are unit-independent facilitate the
comparison of model performance across datasets with varying
scales [45]. This is particularly important for normalizing errors
in CPU usage predictions across VMs with fluctuating workloads.
By employing these metrics, it can uniformly assess errors, iden-
tify anomalies, and further enhance the accuracy and reliability
of CPU usage forecasts. Research [46] has demonstrated the sta-
tistical significance of these metrics in evaluating deep learning
models for time-series forecasting. Given their effectiveness in
this context, we therefore apply MAPE, RMSE, and WAPE in our
evaluation to understand model performance and to determine
which algorithm provides higher predictive accuracy across dif-
ferent VMs.
4.3
|
Experimental Setup
The proposed AINet0 framework was implemented and tested
on CloudAIBus [33], which is an AI-based testbed designed to
improve resource allocation in cloud environments. CloudAIBus
can function as a flexible framework for integrating and testing
predictive models. In our study, we advanced research by utiliz-
ing Amazon Forecast instead of Google Colab to implement the
experiments. The experimental setup involved configuring the
AWS environment, preparing historical CPU usage data stored
in the S3 bucket, and using Amazon Forecast to build and evalu-
ate predictive models for CPU usage across VMs. Two advanced
forecasting algorithms, including DeepAR+ and CNN-QR, were
trained with a 30-minute forecast horizon and evaluated using
key metrics (MAPE, RMSE, and WAPE) to assess their accuracy
in predicting future CPU usage.
4.4
|
Results
Figure 6 compares the performance of DeepAR+ and CNN-QR
based on three key metrics such as MAPE, RMSE, and
WAPE. CNN-QR outperforms DeepAR+ with a lower MAPE of
0.0648 versus 0.1300, indicating more accurate percentage-error
predictions.
CNN-QR also achieves a slightly lower RMSE of 49.8639 com-
pared to DeepAR+’s 54.4374, suggesting its forecasts tend to
be closer to the actual values and reduce the impact of larger
errors. In terms of WAPE, CNN-QR achieves 0.0744 compared
to DeepAR+’s 0.1015, further demonstrating its effectiveness
in minimizing errors relative to the scale of actual values.
CNN-QR has delivered precise and reliable forecasts, minimizing
errors and ensuring accurate short-term predictions. The choice
between these models depends on the specific requirements of
the forecasting task, such as capturing complex patterns or min-
imizing errors.

|

reflecting significant prediction errors and limitations in captur-

all compared models, achieving an exceptionally low MAPE of
6.48%, which demonstrates its superior accuracy and reliability in
minimizing forecast errors. Furthermore, CNN-QR’s probabilis-
tic forecasting via quantile regression makes it especially efficient

Discussions
In this paper, we evaluated the performance of two forecasting
models, DeepAR+ and CNN-QR, to predict the CPU usage on
VMs. Accurate CPU usage predictions are critical for efficient
resource allocation and performance management in virtualized
environments.
The DeepAR+ model (see Figure 8) provides a stable forecast,
with the P10, P50, and P90 percentiles displaying a relatively
narrow range. For instance, the model predicts an increase in
CPU utilization after 10:00 p.m., with the P90 forecast reaching
around 20 MHz and the P10 forecast around 15 MHz. This nar-
row range indicates high reliability and consistency, highlighting
DeepAR+’s suitability for environments with predictable work-
loads, where stable resource provisioning is essential. In contrast,
the CNN-QR model (see Figure 9) captures a broader range of
potential CPU usage scenarios. Initially, the target value remains
steady until a drop at 9:56 p.m., after which the predictions
vary; the P50 forecast stabilizes around 10 MHz. The wider range
between P10 and P90 reflects CNN-QR’s sensitivity to rapid fluc-
tuations, allowing CNN-QR to accommodate non-linear changes
and sudden spikes in demand, potentially preventing resource
shortages during unexpected activity bursts.
Collectively, these models demonstrate distinct strengths, with
DeepAR+ offering stable and narrow forecasts ideal for steady
and predictable environments, while CNN-QR provides flexi-
ble predictions that capture variability in dynamic settings. The
selection between these models should be determined by the spe-
cific operational requirements, such as stability for consistent
workloads versus adaptability for highly variable demands.
5
|
Conclusions and Future Work
In this research, we developed the AINet0 framework employing
DeepAR+ and CNN-QR models available on Amazon Forecast to
enable carbon-neutral cloud resource management. By analysing
historical CPU usage from the GWA-T-12 dataset, our framework
accurately predicts future demand, thereby optimizing resource
allocation. Experimental results indicate that our proposed mod-
els significantly outperform classical methods, with the CNN-QR
model achieving a MAPE of 6.48% and DeepAR+ attaining 13%.
These improvements in prediction accuracy help reduce both
over-provisioning and under-provisioning of resources. While
DeepAR+ is well suited for stable and predictable environ-
ments, CNN-QR proves more effective in dynamic settings with
unpredictable workloads. Overall, our approach improves cloud
resource management, promoting more carbon-neutral opera-
tions, contributing toward net-zero emission targets.

Abstract: Cloud computing is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to optimize resource management and address the complex and fluctuating demands of modern cloud environments. In particular, accurate CPU usage prediction-achieved through appropriate time-series forecasting, is crucial for minimizing both over-provisioning and under-provisioning of cloud resources. High predictive accuracy not only mitigates operational inefficiencies but also aligns with net-zero emission goals by reducing unnecessary energy consumption. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework AINet0, which uses AI forecasting models such as neural networks and time-series models for a dynamic resource management approach. The AINet0 integrates and examines Amazon’s DeepAR+ and Convolutional Neural Network-Quantile Regression (CNN-QR) within the Amazon Web Services environment, aiming to enhance energy efficiency and sustainability to enable carbon-neutral cloud ser- vices. We evaluated the AINet0 framework using a real testbed, CloudAIBus, and compared its performance against established baselines. The experimental results demonstrate that the AINet0 enhances forecasting accuracy, achieving lower metrics such as Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), allowing for more precise resource allocation. Furthermore, performance evaluation conducted on the Grid Workload Archive-T-12 dataset shows that the proposed models outperform traditional methods, enabling more sustainable and cost-effective operations that further support net-zero emissions objectives.
